storm.summary_layperson: A slow-moving low pressure system is bringing waves of showers and thunderstorms into the area from the west through this afternoon, and the Sound isn't cool enough right now to offer the cove much extra protection compared to nearby towns.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound is only about 5°F cooler than the air today (74°F water vs 79°F air) — too weak a marine layer to reliably choke storms before they reach the cove.
storm.detail_html:
A slow-moving area of low pressure is spreading multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms across the region today into Wednesday, moving in from the west in south-to-north bands. The National Weather Service's Upton office is watching for an isolated damaging wind threat with instability in the 1000–2000 J/kg range (measured locally at 1640 J/kg) — enough for a collapsing storm to produce a gust over 40 kt, even without organized severe structure. A Flood Watch is in effect for the area through Wednesday evening given the repeated rounds of heavy rain.

The cove's usual defense — a stable marine layer over a cool Sound — is only weakly in play today. Water is 74°F against 79°F air, a 4.5°F delta that falls short of the threshold where the pipeline calls the protective mechanism "active." Shear is also weak (around 10 kt at the moment, drifting toward the mid-teens through the afternoon), which normally favors the marine layer choking updrafts — but the marine layer itself just isn't strong enough today to lean on.

Net effect: the cove should expect roughly the same storm exposure as Riverside, Old Greenwich, and the rest of the immediate shoreline — no meaningful local discount, but also no local amplification. Radar is currently clear of cells within range, so nothing is imminent as of this fetch (scan at 11:25 AM).

What would change the call: any cell showing up on KOKX radar within 50 miles at or above 35 dBZ would push this to "moderate" territory with a specific radar picture attached (it already qualifies as moderate on the Flood Watch + destabilizing-trend criteria alone); a cell within 25 miles at 45+ dBZ heading toward the cove, or an upgrade to a severe thunderstorm warning, would push it to "high." Watch for the heavier bands mentioned in the forecast moving in from the west later this afternoon and evening.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light-to-moderate gradient wind, not a sea-breeze day — direction backs from S to SE through the window as pressure gradually favors the west shore. Start center-line, then work right (west) as the day backs toward SE.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day: the air–water temperature difference is only 4.5°F, short of the 5°F gate the thermal sea breeze needs, even though 67% of coastal stations are currently reading southerly. With that gate unmet, the wind you're sailing in is straight synoptic flow (mean authoritative wind speed 9.4 kt), not a locally-driven thermal — that's the moderate gradient wind call, no maturation correction to apply.

Direction backs steadily through the window: S (190°) at the top of the hour, easing through SSE by early afternoon, reaching SE (142°) by 3 PM. That's a persistent shift, not an oscillating one — there's no mature thermal cycling here, just the wind vein rotating ahead of the approaching low pressure system. Play it as a one-way bet on the correct side rather than tacking on headers.

Cove geography: pure S flow (the late-morning hours) is fairly uniform across the course, maybe a touch stronger on the east side near the mouth. But as direction backs into SSE–SE for the early afternoon, Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) starts sheltering the east side of the course, and pressure shifts to favor the west shore — work right as the hours pass.

Model/obs check: HRRR's current-hour direction (190°) is only 6° off the live station ensemble (196°) — a minor divergence, nothing that needs a manual override.

Speed-wise this is a light day for dinghies — 5–9 kt with gusts to 13 kt, a drifter-to-light-air day, not a big-breeze one. The wrinkle: a slow-moving low is bringing chance-of-thunderstorm hours right through the middle of this window (11 AM–2 PM per NWS), and any storm cell that fires could punch a gust well above 40 kt per the local AFD — those numbers won't show up in the steady-state HRRR table above. Keep an eye on the sky, not just the forecast table.
